title: B-Tree vs LSM-Tree: why Cassandra writes 10x faster than Postgres

meta.yt_title: Why Cassandra Writes 10x Faster Than MySQL (B-Tree vs LSM-Tree) #shorts
meta.yt_description:
Why do write-heavy systems replace B-Trees with LSM-Trees? Sequential I/O.

• B-Trees (PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB) update 8KB or 16KB pages in-place, causing heavy random disk I/O
• LSM-Trees (Cassandra, RocksDB) append writes sequentially into an in-memory MemTable and Write-Ahead Log
• When full, MemTables flush as immutable SSTables to disk
• Sequential disk writes run at hardware speed, eliminating random seek bottlenecks

Voiceover is AI-generated. Source: Martin Kleppmann (DDIA), Apache Cassandra Architecture.
meta.ig_caption:
Why can Cassandra write 10x faster than MySQL or Postgres? ⚡

It comes down to storage engines:

🌳 B-Trees (MySQL/Postgres) update pages in-place. Every write causes random disk I/O and page fragmentation.

⚡ LSM-Trees (Cassandra/RocksDB) never overwrite disk pages. Writes append sequentially into an in-memory MemTable.

Sequential disk I/O is up to 100x faster than random writes.

Follow @stackshade for more.

Voiceover is AI-generated. Source: Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Cassandra docs.

scenes.say: Traditional databases use B-Trees. Every insert modifies an eight or sixteen kilobyte page in place, causing random disk I/O.
Cassandra and RocksDB use LSM-Trees. Writes never modify disk pages in place. They append sequentially to memory.

els.text: Sequential append to RAM, flushed as SSTables.

scenes.say: LSM-Trees trade slower reads for blazing writes. That is why high-throughput systems choose them. Follow StackShade for more.
